nameStory: Livoneca ovalis gets its scientific name from its oval-shaped body - 'ovalis' literally means 'egg-shaped' in Latin. The genus name Livoneca comes from a combination of Latin words, though this particular fish parasite doesn't have a widely-used common name since most people never see them unless they're cleaning fish.
description: Livoneca ovalis is a parasitic crustacean that lives inside the mouths and gill chambers of marine fish, particularly menhaden and other herring-like species. These bizarre creatures look like flattened, segmented pills or tiny armadillos, typically measuring about half an inch to an inch long. They're actually related to the familiar pill bugs you find under logs, but these have adapted to a life of latching onto fish gills and feeding on blood and mucus. Their bodies are whitish to pale yellow, with seven pairs of legs that help them grip onto their unfortunate hosts.

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Distinctly oval and flattened from top to bottom, like a small, segmented pancake with visible body segments running crosswise

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: About the size of a large pea to small grape, typically 0.5 to 1 inch long when fully grown

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale whitish, cream, or yellowish color that may appear somewhat translucent when fresh

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Seven pairs of small, hook-like legs along the underside that feel rough and grabby to the touch

idTips.label: Location on fish
idTips.description: Found attached inside the fish's mouth, throat, or gill chamber - never on the outside skin

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Firm and slightly rubbery feeling, not squishy like a worm, with a hard segmented shell

habitat: You'll only encounter Livoneca ovalis when cleaning saltwater fish caught in New England's coastal waters, particularly in warmer months. They prefer fish hosts like menhaden, herring, and related species that swim in schools in nearshore waters from Massachusetts to Connecticut. Look for them when filleting fish caught in bays, harbors, and within a few miles of shore.

seasonality.spring: More commonly found in fish as waters warm up and parasite activity increases. Spring-caught menhaden and herring may harbor these parasites as they move into nearshore waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for finding these parasites in fish, as warm water temperatures promote their growth and reproduction. Most encounters happen during summer fishing season.
seasonality.fall: Still active in fish catches during early fall, though numbers may decline as water temperatures drop and fish migrate.
seasonality.winter: Rarely encountered in winter catches, as both the parasites and their preferred fish hosts are less active in cold New England waters.

funFact: These parasites can actually replace a fish's tongue - they attach to the base of the tongue, cause it to wither away, and then function as a living prosthetic tongue, helping the fish eat while simultaneously feeding on its blood and mucus!
confusionNotes: Most people might mistake these for some kind of grub or larva when first encountered, but remember that parasitic isopods are hard-shelled crustaceans with visible legs, while fly larvae or other grubs are soft-bodied and legless. The segmented, armadillo-like appearance is the giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: Many anglers are startled to find these 'alien-looking' creatures in their fish, but they're actually quite common and the fish meat is still perfectly safe to eat. These parasites don't affect humans and are easily removed during normal fish cleaning - they're just one of nature's more unsettling examples of parasitism.
compareHints: **Note: Limited reference material available for this species** Since Livoneca ovalis appears to be the only member of its genus commonly found in New England waters, compare it to other fish parasites like sea lice (which are external and much smaller) or fish tapeworms (which are internal but ribbon-like and soft). The hard, segmented, oval body with visible legs makes Livoneca unique among fish parasites you're likely to encounter.
